prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how trade reallocates resources across firms and shapes the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework meets the criteria I would apply in any field. It replaced the representative-firm assumption with a mechanism (selection into exporting, within-industry reallocation) that generates sharp, testable predictions. Those predictions have been checked repeatedly across countries and datasets, and the core qualitative patterns have held up. The framework also created a shared empirical toolkit built on firm-level data, and it is used in policy evaluation. Melitz (2003) is a clearly identifiable originating contribution. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, and his earlier trade theory, make him the natural second laureate. After more than two decades of replication and extension, I can judge this body of work on how well it has survived testing, not only on how influential it has been.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the main weakness. The parallel firm-level empirical work by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is not credited on this ballot entry, so a Melitz-Helpman prize could be seen as under-crediting the empirical foundations. Some welfare and gains-from-trade results depend on functional-form choices such as Pareto-distributed productivity. Trade also received a prize in 2008, though that is a question of field balance and not of scientific merit.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks law and finance first. He grants that the legal-origins measurement has been criticised but argues the paradigm's reach across corporate finance, law and development is exceptional, and he acknowledges that excluding Vishny is a real attribution cost.
responses.response: I agree the programme's reach is exceptional and that it opened a large research area. Reach and robustness are different things, though, and I ranked it seventh for that reason. The causal reading of legal origin, the coding of the anti-director indices and the endogeneity of legal origin remain contested. The core predictions of the firm-heterogeneity framework have survived testing better. Where the evidence is weaker than the influence, I would count that against the candidate. I share your concern about Vishny. The three-name cap makes law and finance harder to define cleanly, whereas Melitz and Helpman are a natural pair.

responses.point: Boppart proposes adding Redding as a third laureate on the trade entry. He sees firm heterogeneity as the basis for modern quantitative trade work and notes that credit is diffuse because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the entry.
responses.response: I take the point that quantitative trade is a direct descendant of the framework. I would still keep Redding out. His contributions are a later wave that builds on the original discovery, and his separable credit is less clear at this stage. A third name would also not fix the real attribution gap, which concerns those outside the ballot entry. I share your worry about diffuse credit. I would rather keep the citation narrowly about the heterogeneous-firm model and selection than stretch it to cover the whole quantitative-trade programme.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks the trade entry second. She notes that credit may be contested by the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line and that trade was recognised in 2008, so the committee might prefer other fields this year.
responses.response: I accept the first concern. The Bernard et al. line deserves careful treatment in the citation wording, and I would phrase it around the theoretical mechanism of selection and reallocation. On the second concern, I would not let an earlier trade prize count against this work. Krugman's prize covered new trade theory with representative firms, and this is a distinct advance. Under common criteria across fields, field rotation is not scientific evidence. The case should rest on discovery, attribution and maturity.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the credit-cycles entry first and the trade entry second. He sees Kiyotaki and Moore as the core, with Gertler as the strongest complement, and he treats Melitz as the clear originator of the heterogeneous-firm model.
responses.response: I agree on Melitz's role as originator, and I ranked Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler second myself. I still prefer the trade entry as the lead for two reasons. The collateral-constraint mechanism is cleanly attributable, but its direct empirical identification is harder than the theory's influence suggests, and the financial-accelerator strand overlaps with the 2022 prize. Gertler's credit is also split with the New Keynesian entry. I do consider it a close call and would keep it as my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants the citation to cover the empirical firm-level trade literature (Bernard, Jensen and others outside this ballot entry) alongside the theory.
How much of the gains-from-trade result depends on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity.
Whether Redding's quantitative contributions should be treated as part of the same discovery or as a later separable one.
Helpman's credit also appears in other candidate packages outside the shortlist, which could split support or complicate attribution.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It records Harvard appointments (2006-17) and a Harvard evolutionary-dynamics network, but documents no tie to the credited candidates.
